trial_name: Annane — Hydrocortisone and Fludrocortisone in Septic Shock (2002)
citation: Annane D, Sébille V, Charpentier C, Bollaert P-E, François B, Korach J-M, et al. Effect of treatment with low doses of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone on mortality in patients with septic shock. JAMA. 2002;288(7):862-871.
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group
one_liner: 7-day low-dose hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone significantly reduced 28-day mortality and accelerated vasopressor withdrawal in corticotropin nonresponders with severe septic shock.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with early catecholamine-dependent septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation.
pico.intervention: Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours (200 mg/day) plus enteral fludrocortisone 50 µg once daily for 7 days.
pico.comparison: Matched IV placebo every 6 hours plus matched enteral placebo once daily for 7 days.

background.existing_knowledge: Earlier high-dose corticosteroid strategies failed to improve survival and raised safety concerns, but septic shock was conceptualised as a state of relative adrenal insufficiency causing vasoplegia.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether stress-dose steroids and mineralocorticoids improve survival and shock reversal, and whether corticotropin testing can target therapy.
background.hypothesis: In early catecholamine-dependent septic shock, 7-day replacement therapy with hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone improves 28-day survival distribution in corticotropin nonresponders.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial stratified by centre (block size 4).
methods.setting: 19 adult ICUs in France; enrolment from April 1995 to March 1999.

inclusion: Adult ICU patients requiring mechanical ventilation
Systolic arterial pressure <90 mm Hg despite fluid resuscitation
Need for vasopressors >=1 hour (dopamine >=15 µg/kg/min or epinephrine/norepinephrine >0.2 µg/kg/min)
Arterial lactate >2 mmol/L (added after protocol amendment)
Enrolled within 3 hours of shock onset (later amended to 8 hours)
exclusion: Etomidate within 6 hours prior to inclusion
Recent ketoconazole, rifampin, phenytoin, or phenobarbital use

methods.intervention: Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours (200 mg/day) plus enteral fludrocortisone 50 µg once daily for 7 days.
methods.comparison: Matched IV placebo every 6 hours plus matched enteral placebo once daily for 7 days.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (patients, clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors) using indistinguishable study drugs in sequentially numbered boxes.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 270 patients to detect a 20% absolute difference in 28-day mortality in corticotropin nonresponders with 90% power (one-sided 5% significance; assumed 95% placebo nonresponder mortality and 40% nonresponder frequency). 300 randomized, 299 analyzed after 1 post-randomisation consent withdrawal.
methods.primary_outcome: 28-day survival distribution in corticotropin nonresponders (nonresponse defined as serum cortisol increase <=9 µg/dL after 250 µg tetracosactrin test).
secondary_outcomes: Survival distribution in all patients and corticotropin responders
methods.follow_up: 28 days (primary), ICU discharge, hospital discharge, and 1 year.

headline_bullets: Primary endpoint (28-day survival distribution in corticotropin nonresponders) was significantly improved with steroids (HR 0.67; P=0.02).
Vasopressor withdrawal was significantly faster in nonresponders receiving steroids (median 7 vs 10 days; HR 1.91; P=0.001).
No survival benefit was observed among corticotropin responders (Adjusted OR 0.97; P=0.96).
Predefined steroid-related adverse events were similar between groups (21% vs 22%; P=0.89).

outcomes_table.note: Median time to death 24 days vs 12 days
Median time to death 19.5 days vs 13 days
Median 7 days vs 10 days; counts reflect withdrawn by day 28
Median 7 days vs 9 days; counts reflect withdrawn by day 28
Direction favoured steroids; mechanistic significance uncertain

subgroup_table.note: Log-rank P=0.81 for survival distribution; log-rank P=0.49 for vasopressor withdrawal (median 3 vs 3.5 days)

safety: Composite steroid-attributable adverse events: 21% (32/150) in steroid group vs 22% (33/149) in placebo group (P=0.89)
Superinfection: 12% in steroid group vs 13% in placebo group
Gastrointestinal bleeding: 7% in steroid group vs 5% in placebo group
Psychiatric disorders: 2% in steroid group vs 5% in placebo group
Wound infection: 0% (0/150) in steroid group vs 5% (7/149) in placebo group (P=0.007)

domains.notes: Central randomisation list with blocks of 4, stratified by centre; allocation concealed via sequentially numbered drug boxes.
Double-blind design using matched IV and enteral placebos.
300 randomised, 1 excluded for post-randomisation consent withdrawal; 299 analyzed on ITT basis. 1 patient died before receiving drug but was analyzed.
High adherence: 150/150 steroid arm and 148/149 placebo arm received study drug. Open-label steroid crossover was not reported.

Well balanced: SAPS II 57±18 vs 60±18, LOD 7.8±3.1 vs 7.9±2.7, lactate 4.3±3.4 vs 4.6±3.0 mmol/L, time from shock to vasopressors 3.5±2.2 vs 3.7±2.2 hours, vasopressor duration before drug 4.1±3.0 vs 4.1±2.4 hours, appropriate antibiotics 91% vs 95%, time to appropriate antibiotics 7.1±10.4 vs 6.0±7.3 hours.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong given concealed allocation, double blinding, objective endpoints, and balanced baselines, though limited by unmeasured co-interventions.

domains.notes: Enrolled highly acute, mechanically ventilated patients in severe catecholamine-dependent shock (76-77% corticotropin nonresponder rate).
Conducted 1995-1999 prior to modern sepsis care bundles; excluded recent steroid and etomidate use.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate: applicable to high-acuity vasopressor-dependent septic shock, but translation is limited by changes in standard sepsis care since 1999.

strengths: Rigorous double-blind randomised design with concealed allocation
Early intervention in severe catecholamine-dependent shock
Objective time-to-event endpoints and near-complete 1-year follow-up
limitations: Primary benefit isolated to corticotropin nonresponders, with a higher nonresponder rate (76-77%) than anticipated
One-sided power calculation based on high mortality assumptions
Small responder subgroup (n=70) limiting statistical power
Lack of reporting on co-interventions and open-label steroid crossovers

critical_appraisal.summary: High-quality landmark RCT proving survival and hemodynamic benefits of replacement-dose corticosteroids in severe septic shock nonresponders to corticotropin.
strengths: Double-dummy blinding ensuring robust performance bias control
Clear separation in time to vasopressor withdrawal
weaknesses: Omission of open-label steroid crossover reporting

sections.authors_conclusion: A 7-day treatment with low doses of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone significantly reduces mortality and speeds shock reversal in patients with septic shock and relative adrenal insufficiency.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone accelerates shock reversal and reduces 28-day mortality in severe, persistent vasopressor-dependent septic shock.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with early, severe, catecholamine-dependent septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Corticotropin stimulation testing must be performed before starting stress-dose steroids.
implementation_caveats: Modern practice uses hydrocortisone without routine ACTH stimulation testing
The incremental necessity of enteral fludrocortisone over hydrocortisone alone remains variable in clinical practice

controversies.notes: Annane established corticotropin nonresponse as a criteria for steroid benefit, but subsequent trials (CORTICUS) found ACTH testing did not predict treatment responsiveness.
Whether fludrocortisone is required alongside hydrocortisone remains debated; APROCCHSS supported dual therapy while ADRENAL showed benefit with hydrocortisone alone.

context_related_trials.relation: Evaluated hydrocortisone alone; showed faster shock reversal but no overall survival benefit and found ACTH response did not modify treatment effect.
Evaluated hydrocortisone continuous infusion in septic shock; demonstrated faster shock reversal and less ICU time but no 90-day mortality reduction.
Evaluated hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone; demonstrated reduced 90-day mortality and increased vasopressor-free days, supporting combination therapy.

unresolved_questions: Is enteral fludrocortisone required when hydrocortisone is administered at stress doses?
Can genomic or inflammatory biomarkers replace corticotropin stimulation testing to guide steroid therapy?

numbers_to_remember: Vasopressor withdrawal time: median 7 vs 10 days (HR 1.91)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Stress-dose hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone speeds shock reversal and reduces 28-day mortality in severe vasopressor-dependent septic shock.
